Fredholm boundary problems with first-order Calderón defects

A boundary parametrix can be Fredholm even when its Calderón matrix is only a projection to leading order. The point is to keep the first lower-order defect in every formula. That defect gains one derivative, compact Sobolev inclusion handles it at the base level, and a separate cancellation makes the boundary right error smoothing.

This lesson builds the full argument. It starts with the original two measurement scales, proves extension regularity, derives both ordered Green errors, constructs the projected boundary inverse, checks all five anisotropic error maps, and proves regularity for solutions and dual obstructions. The final result is a Fredholm realization whose index is independent of Sobolev level and lower-order terms.

Named prerequisites are Inverting mixed symbols without changing their scales, Composing symbols with two independent orders, Sobolev mapping with normal and tangential weights, Finite inverse expansions for normal polynomials, Cauchy data from jumps and residues, Solving an elliptic system from compatible boundary measurements, and Finite defects under perturbation. We use each result only with its stated hypotheses.

1. The operator, the two weights, and the boundary spaces

Let XX be a compact smooth manifold with boundary YY, and fix an inward collar coordinate t≥0t\geq0. Let E→XE\to X and F→XF\to X have the same finite rank. Near YY, the generalized interior operator has the ordered normal form

Pb=∑a=0mPa(y,t,Dy)Dta,ord⁡DyPa≤m−a,Pm(y,t):E(y,t)→F(y,t) invertible.(GF1) P^b=\sum_{a=0}^{m}P_a(y,t,D_y)D_t^a, \qquad \operatorname{ord}_{D_y}P_a\leq m-a, \qquad P_m(y,t):E_{(y,t)}\longrightarrow F_{(y,t)} \text{ invertible}. \tag{GF1}

The tangential entries are classical pseudodifferential operators. The interior term PiP^i is supported away from the collar, and P=Pb+PiP=P^b+P^i has an elliptic extension to a boundaryless neighborhood X̂\widehat X. In a collar chart its complete left symbol p(x,η,ζ)p(x,\eta,\zeta) and inverse symbol τ(x,η,ζ)\tau(x,\eta,\zeta) use the numerical symbol weights

R=1+|(η,ζ)|,T=1+|η|,∥∂xβ∂ηα∂ζra∥≤CβαrRu−rTv−|α|(GF2) R=1+|(\eta,\zeta)|, \qquad T=1+|\eta|, \qquad \|\partial_x^\beta\partial_\eta^\alpha\partial_\zeta^r a\| \leq C_{\beta\alpha r}R^{u-r}T^{v-|\alpha|} \tag{GF2}

for a∈Su,va\in S^{u,v}. The Sobolev norms retain the distinct quadratic weights

Q=(1+|η|2+ζ2)1/2,h=(1+|η|2)1/2,∥u∥(s,t)2=(2π)−n∫Q2sh2t|û|2.(GF3) Q=(1+|\eta|^2+\zeta^2)^{1/2}, \qquad h=(1+|\eta|^2)^{1/2}, \qquad \|u\|_{(s,t)}^2=(2\pi)^{-n}\int Q^{2s}h^{2t}|\widehat u|^2. \tag{GF3}

The complete constructions in Sections 14–18 and the full-extension correction in Section 23 give proper global operators Τ=Op⁡(τ)\Tau=\operatorname{Op}(\tau), RER_E, and RFR_F, with matrix multiplication in the displayed order, such that

ΤP=I+RE,PΤ=I+RF,rE,rF∈S−1,0.(GF4) \Tau P=I+R_E, \qquad P\Tau=I+R_F, \qquad r_E,r_F\in S^{-1,0}. \tag{GF4}

Section 20 proves the stronger finite decompositions MH1–MH19 and their one-sided estimates, including boundary-supported inputs. For the first inverse, take N=1 in the actual finite construction:

r+Τe+:H‾(s,t)→H‾(s+m,t),r+REe+,r+RFe+:H‾(s,t)→H‾(s+1,t)(s≥0),(GF5) \begin{aligned} r^+\Tau e^+&:\bar H_{(s,t)}\longrightarrow\bar H_{(s+m,t)},\\ r^+R_Ee^+,\ r^+R_Fe^+&:\bar H_{(s,t)}\longrightarrow\bar H_{(s+1,t)} \qquad(s\geq0), \end{aligned} \tag{GF5}

and, whenever w∈H(−m,r)(X̂)w\in H_{(-m,r)}(\widehat X) is supported on YY,

r+Τw∈H‾(ν,r−ν),r+REw,r+RFw∈H‾(ν+1−m,r−ν)(ν∈ℝ).(GF6) \begin{aligned} r^+\Tau w&\in\bar H_{(\nu,r-\nu)},\\ r^+R_Ew,\ r^+R_Fw&\in\bar H_{(\nu+1-m,r-\nu)} \end{aligned} \qquad(\nu\in\mathbb R). \tag{GF6}

All constants in (GF5)–(GF6) are finite combinations of the source R,TR,T seminorms; the spaces themselves are the Q,hQ,h spaces (GF3).

Write γku=(Dtku)|Y\gamma_k u=(D_t^ku)|_Y, 0≤k<m0\leq k<m, and γu=(γ0u,…,γm−1u)\gamma u=(\gamma_0u,\ldots,\gamma_{m-1}u). For real rr, set

𝒞r=⨁k=0m−1Hr−k−1/2(Y,E),𝒟r=⨁j=1JHr−mj−1/2(Y,Gj).(GF7) \mathcal C^r=\bigoplus_{k=0}^{m-1}H^{r-k-1/2}(Y,E), \qquad \mathcal D^r=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{J}H^{r-m_j-1/2}(Y,G_j). \tag{GF7}

Let Bj=∑k<mBjkγkB_j=\sum_{k<m}B_{jk}\gamma_k, where Bjk∈Ψmj−k(Y;E,Gj)B_{jk}\in\Psi^{m_j-k}(Y;E,G_j), and write ℬ=(Bjk)\mathcal B=(B_{jk}). The complementing condition says that the principal boundary matrix bb is a fiberwise bijection from the stable Cauchy bundle onto ⨁jGj\bigoplus_jG_j.

2. Elliptic regularity on the extension

Let u∈Hcomps+m−1(X̂,E)u\in H^{s+m-1}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat X,E) and Pu∈Hcomps(X̂,F)Pu\in H^s_{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat X,F). Choose chart cutoffs χ≺η\chi\prec\eta, so η=1\eta=1 on a neighborhood of supp⁡χ\operatorname{supp}\chi. With [P,η]=Pη−ηP[P,\eta]=P\eta-\eta P, (GF4) gives on that chart

χu=χΤ(ηPu)+χΤ([P,η]u)−χRE(ηu)+Gχu.(GF8) \chi u =\chi\Tau(\eta Pu)+\chi\Tau([P,\eta]u) -\chi R_E(\eta u)+G_\chi u. \tag{GF8}

Here Gχ=0G_\chi=0: apply the exact first identity of (GF4) to ηu\eta u and then multiply by χ\chi. Section 23 proves that tangentially separated mixed kernels can remain singular in the normal coordinate; their contribution stays in the full commutator. The commutator has generalized order m−1m-1: each normal commutator lowers the normal differential degree once, and each tangential commutator lowers the tangential pseudodifferential order once. U030 and (GF5) therefore give

∥χu∥Hs+m≤Cχ,η,K(∥ηPu∥Hs+∥u∥Hs+m−1).(GF9) \|\chi u\|_{H^{s+m}} \leq C_{\chi,\eta,K} \bigl(\|\eta Pu\|_{H^s}+\|u\|_{H^{s+m-1}}\bigr). \tag{GF9}

The lower norm in (GF9) retains the entire input, including distant tangential components. The exact counterexample ML1–ML5 in Section 23 disproves the stronger estimate with only ηu\eta u in that norm. In the overlap, invert the complete symbol of Pb+PiP^b+P^i; ellipticity of PP alone does not prove ellipticity of PiP^i there. Use ordinary interior charts only where the collar summand vanishes. ML6–ML8 gives both ordered full-extension errors. A finite partition of unity over a fixed compact K⊃supp⁡uK\supset\operatorname{supp}u proves

u∈Hcomps+m(X̂),∥u∥Hs+m≤CK(∥Pu∥Hs+∥u∥Hs+m−1).(GF10) u\in H^{s+m}_{\mathrm{comp}}(\widehat X), \qquad \|u\|_{H^{s+m}} \leq C_K\bigl(\|Pu\|_{H^s}+\|u\|_{H^{s+m-1}}\bigr). \tag{GF10}

This proves extension regularity in the generalized class. Repeating (GF10) raises any distributional solution with smooth right side through all real Sobolev orders, one full derivative at a time.

3. The boundary source and two exact Green identities

For a Cauchy vector U=(U0,…,Um−1)U=(U_0,\ldots,U_{m-1}), define the exact boundary distribution

𝒥U=1i∑a=1mPa(y,t,Dy)∑r=0a−1Ua−1−r⊗Dtrδ0.(GF11) \mathcal JU=\frac1i\sum_{a=1}^{m}P_a(y,t,D_y) \sum_{r=0}^{a-1}U_{a-1-r}\otimes D_t^r\delta_0. \tag{GF11}

The coefficient Pa(y,t,Dy)P_a(y,t,D_y) acts after the delta derivative. Expanding that multiplication gives every normal derivative of PaP_a as in U025 (BF20); none is removed. For smooth uu, distributional differentiation of its zero extension gives

P(e+u)=e+(Pu)+𝒥γu.(GF12) P(e^+u)=e^+(Pu)+\mathcal J\gamma u. \tag{GF12}

Define

V=r+Τe+,K=r+Τ𝒥,Q=γK,E=r+REe+,F=r+RFe+,H=r+RF𝒥.(GF13) \begin{gathered} V=r^+\Tau e^+, \qquad K=r^+\Tau\mathcal J, \qquad Q=\gamma K,\\ E=r^+R_Ee^+, \qquad F=r^+R_Fe^+, \qquad H=r^+R_F\mathcal J. \end{gathered} \tag{GF13}

Apply r+Τr^+\Tau to (GF12), then use the first identity in (GF4). Apply PP to the two terms in (GF13), then use the second identity in (GF4) and the fact that r+𝒥U=0r^+\mathcal JU=0. This proves the exact identities

u+Eu=V(Pu)+Kγu,PV=I+F,PK=H.(GF14) u+Eu=V(Pu)+K\gamma u, \qquad PV=I+F, \qquad PK=H. \tag{GF14}

The boundary source estimate is obtained without deleting any delta coefficient. If Uk∈Hr−k−1/2(Y)U_k\in H^{r-k-1/2}(Y), the coefficient of Dtjδ0D_t^j\delta_0 in (GF11) lies in Hr−m+j+1/2H^{r-m+j+1/2}. The full jet representation and cross-term Gram norm MH14–MH17 in Section 20 gives

∥𝒥U∥(−m,r)≤Cr∑k=0m−1∥Uk∥Hr−k−1/2.(GF15) \|\mathcal JU\|_{(-m,r)} \leq C_r\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\|U_k\|_{H^{r-k-1/2}}. \tag{GF15}

Combining (GF6) and (GF15) controls KK, EKE K, VHV H, and all later boundary-source terms for arbitrary real output split.

4. The generalized Calderón matrix

Write the full homogeneous principal polynomial, without identifying it with its leading normal coefficient, as

𝔭(y,η,ζ)=∑a=0mpa,m−a(y,η)ζa.(GF16a) \mathfrak p(y,\eta,\zeta) =\sum_{a=0}^{m}p_{a,m-a}(y,\eta)\zeta^a. \tag{GF16a}

Sections 21 and 24 prove that the entries of QQ satisfy Qkl∈Ψk−l(Y;E,E)Q_{kl}\in\Psi^{k-l}(Y;E,E), including the full source and every output derivative. PC1–PC7 compares the actual inverse with the entire homogeneous polynomial, retaining the lower-order difference. Its weighted principal symbol is

qkl(y,η)=12πi∫Γ+∑j=0m−1−lζk+j𝔭(y,η,ζ)−1pj+l+1,m−j−l−1(y,η)dζ.(GF16) q_{kl}(y,\eta)=\frac1{2\pi i}\int_{\Gamma_+} \sum_{j=0}^{m-1-l}\zeta^{k+j} \mathfrak p(y,\eta,\zeta)^{-1} p_{j+l+1,m-j-l-1}(y,\eta)\,d\zeta. \tag{GF16}

The inverse stands on the left of the coefficient. The jump argument CD23–CD26 applies to this full matrix polynomial and proves that q2=qq^2=q, with range equal to the Cauchy data of the inward-decaying frozen solutions. Consequently

Q2−Q∈Ψwt−1(Y;E⊕m,E⊕m),(GF17) Q^2-Q\in\Psi^{-1}_{\mathrm{wt}}(Y;E^{\oplus m},E^{\oplus m}), \tag{GF17}

where weighted order −1-1 means that the (k,l)(k,l) entry lies in Ψk−l−1\Psi^{k-l-1}. No smoothing conclusion follows from the leading-symbol identity.

There is also an exact operator formula for this defect. Put u=KUu=KU in the first identity of (GF14). Since PKU=HUPKU=HU, take Cauchy traces and obtain

Q2−Q=γEK−γVH.(GF18) Q^2-Q=\gamma E K-\gamma V H. \tag{GF18}

Every term on the right gains one weighted derivative by (GF5), (GF6), and (GF15). This verifies the order in (GF17) from the actual ordered errors.

Put u=Vfu=Vf in the same identity. Since PVf=f+FfPVf=f+Ff, cancellation of VfVf gives

QγVf=γEVf−γVFf.(GF19) Q\gamma Vf=\gamma E Vf-\gamma V Ff. \tag{GF19}

Thus, for s≥0s\geq0,

QγV:H‾(s,t)(X)→⨁k=0m−1Hs+t+m−k+1/2(Y,E).(GF20) Q\gamma V:\bar H_{(s,t)}(X)\longrightarrow \bigoplus_{k=0}^{m-1}H^{s+t+m-k+1/2}(Y,E). \tag{GF20}

The extra derivative in (GF20) comes from both ordered errors in (GF19); it is not obtained by tracing VfVf alone.

7. One derivative at a time for solutions

Let u∈H‾mu\in\bar H^m have bounded collar support, let Pu∈H‾s−mPu\in\bar H^{s-m}, and let Bju∈Hs−mj−1/2B_ju\in H^{s-m_j-1/2}, where s≥ms\geq m. Suppose first that u∈H‾ru\in\bar H^r for some m≤r<sm\leq r<s, and put

r+=min⁡(s,r+1).(GF39) r_+=\min(s,r+1). \tag{GF39}

Choose χ≺η\chi\prec\eta in the collar and apply (GF29) to ηu\eta u. The interior commutator [P,η]u[P,\eta]u has order m−1m-1, so it lies in Hr−m+1⊂Hr+−mH^{r-m+1}\subset H^{r_+-m}. For the boundary rows, write ηa=(Dtaη)|Y\eta_a=(D_t^a\eta)|_Y, so η0=η|Y\eta_0=\eta|_Y, and let MηaM_{\eta_a} denote multiplication by ηa\eta_a. The full normal Leibniz formula is

γk(ηu)=∑a=0k(ka)Mηaγk−au,Bj(ηu)−Mη0Bju=∑k=0m−1[Bjk,Mη0]γku+∑k=0m−1∑a=1k(ka)BjkMηaγk−au.(GF40) \begin{aligned} \gamma_k(\eta u) &=\sum_{a=0}^k\binom ka M_{\eta_a}\gamma_{k-a}u,\\ B_j(\eta u)-M_{\eta_0}B_ju &=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}[B_{jk},M_{\eta_0}]\gamma_ku\\ &\quad+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\sum_{a=1}^k \binom ka B_{jk}M_{\eta_a}\gamma_{k-a}u. \end{aligned} \tag{GF40}

The first line follows by induction from the product rule for DtD_t; applying each BjkB_{jk} and subtracting Mη0∑kBjkγkuM_{\eta_0}\sum_kB_{jk}\gamma_ku gives the remaining lines in the displayed order. The first sum has coefficient order at most mj−k−1m_j-k-1. In the second sum put l=k−al=k-a. Its coefficient has order at most mj−k=mj−l−a≤mj−l−1m_j-k=m_j-l-a\leq m_j-l-1, with every binomial factor and cutoff derivative retained. Thus each coefficient acting on γlu∈Hr−l−1/2\gamma_lu\in H^{r-l-1/2} has output in Hr−mj+1/2⊂Hr+−mj−1/2H^{r-m_j+1/2}\subset H^{r_+-m_j-1/2}. The normal-cutoff terms need not vanish; they satisfy precisely the same weighted order bound. Tangentially separated terms retain their normal-diagonal kernels and the actual lower mixed orders of Sections 14, 18 and 20. The input at this step is known globally in the lower Sobolev space, so the full commutator estimates apply. The data term ℒ(P(ηu),B(ηu))\mathscr L(P(\eta u),B(\eta u)) therefore lies in H‾r+\bar H^{r_+}, while (GF36) puts 𝒦(ηu)\mathscr K(\eta u) in H‾r+1⊂H‾r+\bar H^{r+1}\subset\bar H^{r_+}. Hence χu∈H‾r+\chi u\in\bar H^{r_+}.

Starting with r0=mr_0=m, define ra+1=min⁡(s,ra+1)r_{a+1}=\min(s,r_a+1). After ⌈s−m⌉\lceil s-m\rceil steps, ra=sr_a=s. If s−ms-m is not an integer, the final step has size strictly below one and all inclusions in (GF40) remain valid. A finite collar partition and ordinary interior regularity prove

u∈H‾s(X,E).(GF41) u\in\bar H^s(X,E). \tag{GF41}

This proves the solution bootstrap with the fractional final step and all cutoff commutators included.

8. The dual one-step bootstrap

Assume the following relation on the whole compact manifold and its boundary:

⟨Pu,v⟩X+∑j⟨Bju,hj⟩Y=0for every compactly supported smooth u,(GF42) \langle Pu,v\rangle_X+\sum_j\langle B_ju,h_j\rangle_Y=0 \quad\text{for every compactly supported smooth }u, \tag{GF42}

with

v∈H‾(0,t)(X,F*⊗ΩX),hj∈Ht+mj+1/2−m(Y,Gj*⊗ΩY).(GF43) v\in\bar H_{(0,t)}(X,F^*\otimes\Omega_X), \qquad h_j\in H^{t+m_j+1/2-m}(Y,G_j^*\otimes\Omega_Y). \tag{GF43}

Insert u=ℒ(0,g)u=\mathscr L(0,g) in (GF42) and use (GF30)–(GF32). For smooth global boundary data gg,

h=−𝒦2′v−𝒦4′h.(GF44) h=-\mathscr K_2'v-\mathscr K_4'h. \tag{GF44}

In (GF35), choose its two free parameters to be s=−1s=-1 and t=−t0−1t=-t_{\!0}-1, where t0t_{\!0} denotes the exponent in (GF43). Then

𝒦2:⨁jH−t0+m−mj−3/2→H‾(0,−t0).(GF45) \mathscr K_2: \bigoplus_jH^{-t_{\!0}+m-m_j-3/2} \longrightarrow\bar H_{(0,-t_{\!0})}. \tag{GF45}

hj∈Ht0+1+mj+1/2−m.(GF46) h_j\in H^{t_{\!0}+1+m_j+1/2-m}. \tag{GF46}

Next insert u=ℒ(f,0)u=\mathscr L(f,0). Then

v=−𝒦1′v−𝒦3′h.(GF47) v=-\mathscr K_1'v-\mathscr K_3'h. \tag{GF47}

The pointwise inequality h/Q≤1h/Q\leq1 gives the continuous embedding H(0,t0)↪H(−1,t0+1)H_{(0,t_{\!0})}\hookrightarrow H_{(-1,t_{\!0}+1)}. With s=0s=0, t=−t0−1t=-t_{\!0}-1, (GF37) transposes to

𝒦1′:Ḣ(−1,t0+1)(X¯)→Ḣ(0,t0+1)(X¯).(GF48) \mathscr K_1':\dot H_{(-1,t_{\!0}+1)}(\overline X)\longrightarrow \dot H_{(0,t_{\!0}+1)}(\overline X). \tag{GF48}

𝒦3′:⨁jHt0+mj+1/2−m→Ḣ(0,t0+1)(X¯).(GF49) \mathscr K_3': \bigoplus_jH^{t_{\!0}+m_j+1/2-m} \longrightarrow \dot H_{(0,t_{\!0}+1)}(\overline X). \tag{GF49}

Equations (GF47)–(GF49) prove

v∈H‾(0,t+1),hj∈Ht+1+mj+1/2−m.(GF50) v\in\bar H_{(0,t+1)}, \qquad h_j\in H^{t+1+m_j+1/2-m}. \tag{GF50}

The dual of a restriction space is the supported Sobolev space with negated exponents. Since the normal order of vv is zero, its zero extension is bounded into H(0,t0)H_{(0,t_{\!0})} and has support in X¯\overline X. PC8 proves its embedding into Ḣ(−1,t0+1)(X¯)\dot H_{(-1,t_{\!0}+1)}(\overline X). Thus (GF48)–(GF49) act on that supported zero extension and their output is restricted back to XX. Section 24 proves every pairing, density and extension-independence step in PC8–PC9. The global relation authorizes both parametrix columns; no arbitrary isolated-patch smoothing claim is used.

Iterating (GF50) makes every hjh_j smooth and gives unlimited tangential regularity to vv. After finitely many steps the second mixed exponent is nonnegative, so v∈L2v\in L^2. Tests away from YY show P†v=0P^\dagger v=0 in the interior. The boundary relation can be written

P†e+v=−∑k=0m−1(−1)k(∑jBjk†hj)⊗Dtkδ0.(GF51) P^\dagger e^+v =-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}(-1)^k \left(\sum_jB_{jk}^\dagger h_j\right)\otimes D_t^k\delta_0. \tag{GF51}

Move the normal derivatives of P†P^\dagger to the right. Its leading normal coefficient is the invertible map (−1)mPmt(-1)^mP_m^t. Exactly as in BF40, comparison from Dtm−1δ0D_t^{m-1}\delta_0 downward uniquely determines smooth exterior jets γ0w,…,γm−1w\gamma_0w,\ldots,\gamma_{m-1}w that cancel (GF51). Recursively impose γr(P†w)=0\gamma_r(P^\dagger w)=0 for every r≥0r\geq0; at each stage the new jet has coefficient (−1)mPmt(-1)^mP_m^t, while the tangential pseudodifferential coefficients act on already known smooth fields and therefore preserve smoothness. The convergent Borel construction BF41 realizes these jets on the exterior collar. Then

W=e+v+e−w,P†W∈C∞(GF52) W=e^+v+e^-w, \qquad P^\dagger W\in C^\infty \tag{GF52}

near YY. The full transpose is elliptic and has the same mixed kernel estimates. Applying the corrected full-operator (GF10) repeatedly to P†P^\dagger proves WW, and hence vv, smooth up to the boundary.

9. Closed range and the finite defect spaces

At the base level put

𝒴m=H‾0(X,F)⊕⨁jHm−mj−1/2(Y,Gj),Amu=(Pu,Bu).(GF53) \mathcal Y^m=\bar H^0(X,F)\oplus \bigoplus_jH^{m-m_j-1/2}(Y,G_j), \qquad A_m u=(Pu,Bu). \tag{GF53}

Equations (GF28)–(GF29) give bounded ℒ:𝒴m→H‾m\mathscr L:\mathcal Y^m\to\bar H^m and

I=ℒAm+𝒦,𝒦:H‾m→H‾m+1.(GF54) I=\mathscr L A_m+\mathscr K, \qquad \mathscr K:\bar H^m\longrightarrow\bar H^{m+1}. \tag{GF54}

The inclusion H‾m+1↪H‾m\bar H^{m+1}\hookrightarrow\bar H^m is compact. If the unit ball of ker⁡Am\ker A_m were not compact, choose a sequence in it with no convergent subsequence. Formula (GF54) makes that sequence equal to its 𝒦\mathscr K-image, which does have a convergent subsequence. Hence ker⁡Am\ker A_m is finite-dimensional.

Let un⟂ker⁡Amu_n\perp\ker A_m and suppose AmunA_mu_n is Cauchy. The sequence unu_n is bounded. Otherwise, after passing to a subsequence with ∥un∥→∞\|u_n\|\to\infty, set wn=un/∥un∥w_n=u_n/\|u_n\|. Then Amwn→0A_mw_n\to0, while compactness gives a convergent subsequence of 𝒦wn\mathscr Kw_n. Equation (GF54) makes wnw_n converge to a unit vector w∈ker⁡Amw\in\ker A_m, contradicting wn⟂ker⁡Amw_n\perp\ker A_m. From boundedness, compactness of 𝒦\mathscr K, convergence of ℒAmun\mathscr LA_mu_n, and (GF54), a subsequence of unu_n converges strongly. Applying the same argument to differences shows the whole sequence is Cauchy. Thus ran⁡Am\operatorname{ran}A_m is closed.

For the cokernel use the full right identity (GF30)–(GF32) on the base data space:

Amℒ=I+ℛ,ℛ=(𝒦1𝒦2𝒦3𝒦4):𝒴m→𝒴m.(GF54R) A_m\mathscr L=I+\mathscr R,\qquad \mathscr R= \begin{pmatrix} \mathscr K_1&\mathscr K_2\\ \mathscr K_3&\mathscr K_4 \end{pmatrix}:\mathcal Y^m\longrightarrow\mathcal Y^m. \tag{GF54R}

Every block is compact in this specific space. With 𝒟m\mathcal D^m as in (GF7), (GF34), (GF35), and (GF37) at s=t=0s=t=0, and (GF38), give the factorizations

𝒦1:H‾0(X,F)→H‾1(X,F)↪H‾0(X,F),𝒦2:𝒟m→H‾1(X,F)↪H‾0(X,F),𝒦3:H‾0(X,F)→𝒟m+1↪𝒟m,𝒦4:𝒟m→𝒟m+1↪𝒟m.(GF54M) \begin{aligned} \mathscr K_1&:\bar H^0(X,F)\longrightarrow \bar H^1(X,F)\hookrightarrow\bar H^0(X,F),\\ \mathscr K_2&:\mathcal D^m\longrightarrow \bar H^1(X,F)\hookrightarrow\bar H^0(X,F),\\ \mathscr K_3&:\bar H^0(X,F)\longrightarrow \mathcal D^{m+1}\hookrightarrow\mathcal D^m,\\ \mathscr K_4&:\mathcal D^m\longrightarrow \mathcal D^{m+1}\hookrightarrow\mathcal D^m. \end{aligned} \tag{GF54M}

The first arrows are bounded. The second arrows are compact Sobolev inclusions on the compact XX or YY, with a finite sum over the boundary bundles. The inclusion H‾1(X,F)↪H‾0(X,F)\bar H^1(X,F)\hookrightarrow\bar H^0(X,F) gains a full derivative, including the normal direction. Tangential gain alone would not justify this step. Write the matrix as the sum of its four blocks composed with the bounded coordinate projections and injections of 𝒴m\mathcal Y^m. Composition with bounded maps and finite addition preserve compactness, so ℛ\mathscr R is compact.

We also need compactness of its transpose on the continuous dual, with the original pairings and densities. Here is a proof. For any ε>0\varepsilon>0, take a finite ε\varepsilon-net y1,…,yNy_1,\ldots,y_N for the image of the unit ball under ℛ\mathscr R. Let Πε\Pi_\varepsilon be the orthogonal projection in the Hilbert space 𝒴m\mathcal Y^m onto their span. The distance-minimizing property of orthogonal projection gives ∥ℛ−Πεℛ∥≤ε\|\mathscr R-\Pi_\varepsilon\mathscr R\|\leq\varepsilon. The transpose of Πεℛ\Pi_\varepsilon\mathscr R has finite rank, and ∥T′∥=∥T∥\|T'\|=\|T\| for a bounded map TT: the inequality in one direction follows from the dual norm, and the reverse follows by taking a unit functional attaining the norm of each nonzero vector TxTx in a Hilbert space. Hence ℛ′\mathscr R' is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank maps. Such a limit is compact, because the image of the unit ball has, for every positive radius, a finite net obtained from a sufficiently close finite-rank map; its closure is complete and totally bounded, therefore compact.

Let

Z={z∈(𝒴m)′:⟨Amu,z⟩=0 for every u∈H‾m(X,E)}.(GF54Z) Z=\{z\in(\mathcal Y^m)':\langle A_mu,z\rangle=0 \text{ for every }u\in\bar H^m(X,E)\}. \tag{GF54Z}

This is a closed linear subspace of the dual. Its elements are the pairs (v,h)(v,h) in (GF42) at t=0t=0, with v∈H‾0(X,F*⊗ΩX),hj∈H−m+mj+1/2(Y,Gj*⊗ΩY). v\in\bar H^0(X,F^*\otimes\Omega_X),\qquad h_j\in H^{-m+m_j+1/2}(Y,G_j^*\otimes\Omega_Y). Transposing (GF54R), with no reversal of the block composition omitted, gives

ℒ′Am′=I+ℛ′,z=−ℛ′z(z∈Z).(GF54D) \mathscr L'A_m'=I+\mathscr R',\qquad z=-\mathscr R'z\quad(z\in Z). \tag{GF54D}

The closed unit ball of ZZ is contained in the compact closure of the image of the dual unit ball under −ℛ′-\mathscr R', and it is closed there. It is therefore compact. The fixed-point lemma proved in Exercise 5 now makes ZZ finite-dimensional. Section 8 separately proves its elements smooth; the tangential bootstrap in that section is used for regularity, not compact inclusion. Since the range is closed, the quotient 𝒴m/ran⁡Am\mathcal Y^m/\operatorname{ran}A_m is a Hilbert space isomorphic to its orthogonal complement. Continuous functionals vanishing on the range identify its dual with ZZ, so its dimension equals dim⁡Z\dim Z. Consequently AmA_m is Fredholm.

10. Every Sobolev level and the index

For s≥ms\geq m, define

𝒴s=H‾s−m(X,F)⊕⨁jHs−mj−1/2(Y,Gj),As:H‾s(X,E)→𝒴s.(GF55) \mathcal Y^s=\bar H^{s-m}(X,F)\oplus \bigoplus_jH^{s-m_j-1/2}(Y,G_j), \qquad A_s:\bar H^s(X,E)\longrightarrow\mathcal Y^s. \tag{GF55}

Let ZZ be the finite-dimensional smooth annihilator found at level mm. Necessity in

ran⁡As={(f,g)∈𝒴s:⟨f,v⟩+∑j⟨gj,hj⟩=0 for every (v,h)∈Z}(GF56) \operatorname{ran}A_s =\left\{(f,g)\in\mathcal Y^s: \langle f,v\rangle+\sum_j\langle g_j,h_j\rangle=0 \text{ for every }(v,h)\in Z\right\} \tag{GF56}

follows by density. Conversely, data in the right side belong to 𝒴m\mathcal Y^m, so base-level closed range gives u∈H‾mu\in\bar H^m with Amu=(f,g)A_mu=(f,g). The solution bootstrap (GF41) gives u∈H‾su\in\bar H^s, proving sufficiency. A nullvector has zero smooth data, so the same bootstrap makes it smooth. Hence the kernel and annihilator are the same spaces at every s≥ms\geq m, and

ind⁡As=dim⁡ker⁡Am−dim⁡Z(s≥m).(GF57) \operatorname{ind}A_s=\dim\ker A_m-\dim Z \qquad(s\geq m). \tag{GF57}

Changing PP by generalized order at most m−1m-1, or changing the (j,k)(j,k) boundary entry by order at most mj−k−1m_j-k-1, maps into a Sobolev space one order above the target. Compact Sobolev inclusion makes the resulting change of AsA_s compact, so (GF57) is unchanged. A sufficiently small change of the finite coefficient and symbol seminorms gives a small operator-norm change H‾s→𝒴s\bar H^s\to\mathcal Y^s. Fredholm operators form an open set and their index is locally constant. Uniform invertibility of the interior principal symbol and of (GF21) on the compact cosphere bundle also persists under such a change. This proves the generalized Fredholm and index-stability theorem.

11. A scalar check that detects the retained defect

Take m=1m=1, one boundary component, and suppose the stable symbol is the scalar q=1q=1, while the constructed Calderón operator is

Q=I+A−1,A−1∈Ψ−1(Y),A−1∉Ψ−∞(Y).(GF58) Q=I+A_{-1}, \qquad A_{-1}\in\Psi^{-1}(Y), \qquad A_{-1}\notin\Psi^{-\infty}(Y). \tag{GF58}

Then

Q2−Q=A−1+A−12∈Ψ−1,(GF59) Q^2-Q=A_{-1}+A_{-1}^2\in\Psi^{-1}, \tag{GF59}

and the leading order-minus-one symbol is that of A−1A_{-1}. With B=IB=I, choose a two-sided parametrix TT of Q2Q^2 and set S=QTS=QT. Then BQS−I=Q2T−IBQS-I=Q^2T-I is smoothing, while

QS−S=(Q2−Q)T(GF60) QS-S=(Q^2-Q)T \tag{GF60}

generally remains order −1-1. This model checks the distinction used in (GF23)–(GF25): the boundary right error can be smoothing even though the Calderón and range defects are only one order lower.

12. Exercises with complete solutions

Exercise 1. Recover every entry order after the order reduction

Assume the source Cauchy component kk has weight kk, the target component jj has weight mjm_j, and the conjugated inverse has order zero. Prove that the original entries of SS, S″S'', and R1R_1 have the orders asserted in (GF26).

Solution. The source reduction DaD_a has diagonal entry of order kk, and the target reduction DbD_b has diagonal entry of order mjm_j. Undoing Ŝ=Da−1SDb\widehat S=D_a^{-1}SD_b gives S=DaŜDb−1S=D_a\widehat S D_b^{-1}, so

ord⁡Skj=k−mj.(GF61) \operatorname{ord}S_{kj}=k-m_j. \tag{GF61}

For an endomorphism of the Cauchy vector, both reductions use the source weights, giving ord⁡Skl″=k−l\operatorname{ord}S''_{kl}=k-l. A weighted order-minus-one endomorphism loses one further order, so ord⁡(R1)kl=k−l−1\operatorname{ord}(R_1)_{kl}=k-l-1. These are exactly the degrees in (GF26); no common scalar order replaces the component degrees.

Exercise 2. Derive the cancellation in the boundary right error

Starting only from R0=I−Sℬ−S″R_0=I-S\mathcal B-S'' and 𝒦4=ℬQS−I\mathscr K_4=\mathcal BQS-I, derive (GF33).

Solution. The first identity gives S″=I−Sℬ−R0S''=I-S\mathcal B-R_0. Substitute it without commuting any matrix factors:

ℬ(I+QS″)=ℬ+ℬQ−ℬQSℬ−ℬQR0=ℬQ−𝒦4ℬ−ℬQR0.(GF62) \begin{aligned} \mathcal B(I+QS'') &=\mathcal B+\mathcal BQ-\mathcal BQS\mathcal B-\mathcal BQR_0\\ &=\mathcal BQ-\mathscr K_4\mathcal B-\mathcal BQR_0. \end{aligned} \tag{GF62}

The first correction is smoothing. The second contains R0R_0, whose (k,l)(k,l) entry has order k−l−1k-l-1. Thus the entire correction to ℬQ\mathcal BQ has entry order at most mj−k−1m_j-k-1, which is the derivative gain used in (GF34).

Exercise 3. Check the two free exponents in 𝒦2\mathscr K_2

Let gj∈Ht+m−mj−1/2g_j\in H^{t+m-m_j-1/2}. Use only (GF15), (GF6), and the orders of SS to prove (GF35).

Solution. Formula (GF61) gives (Sg)k∈Ht+m−k−1/2(Sg)_k\in H^{t+m-k-1/2}. Hence (GF15) gives 𝒥Sg∈H(−m,t+m)\mathcal JSg\in H_{(-m,t+m)}. The RFR_F line of (GF6) sends a boundary-supported input in H(−m,r)H_{(-m,r)} to H(ν+1−m,r−ν)H_{(\nu+1-m,r-\nu)}. Set

r=t+m,ν=s+m.(GF63) r=t+m, \qquad \nu=s+m. \tag{GF63}

The output is H(s+1,t−s)H_{(s+1,t-s)}, for arbitrary real s,ts,t. The input exponent contains no ss, exactly as (GF35) states.

Exercise 4. Verify the dual gain for the boundary obstruction

In (GF35), put s=−1s=-1 and replace its second parameter by −t−1-t-1. Compute the transposed map and show that it raises the exponent of hjh_j by one.

Solution. With those parameters, (GF35) becomes

𝒦2:⨁jH−t+m−mj−3/2→H(0,−t).(GF64) \mathscr K_2: \bigoplus_jH^{-t+m-m_j-3/2} \longrightarrow H_{(0,-t)}. \tag{GF64}

Sobolev duality reverses both exponents. Therefore 𝒦2′\mathscr K_2' maps H(0,t)H_{(0,t)} into ⨁jHt+1+mj+1/2−m\bigoplus_jH^{t+1+m_j+1/2-m}. Formula (GF44), together with the smoothing transpose 𝒦4′\mathscr K_4', proves the asserted one-step gain for hh.

Exercise 5. Prove the compact fixed-point lemma used twice above

Let XX be a Banach space, C:X→XC:X\to X compact, and M⊂XM\subset X a linear subspace such that x=Cxx=Cx for every x∈Mx\in M. Prove that MM is finite-dimensional.

Solution. Keep the given subspace MM, and introduce the entire fixed space F=ker⁡(I−C)F=\ker(I-C). It is a closed linear subspace of the Banach space XX, and M⊂FM\subset F. If xn∈Fx_n\in F tends to xx in XX, continuity gives x=Cxx=Cx, which proves x∈Fx\in F; it does not by itself prove membership in the original arbitrary MM.

Let BF={x∈F:∥x∥≤1}B_F=\{x\in F:\|x\|\leq1\}. For every x∈BFx\in B_F, x=Cxx=Cx, so BFB_F is contained in C(BX)C(B_X). It is closed in XX and thus closed in the compact closure of C(BX)C(B_X). Therefore BFB_F is compact.

For completeness, an infinite-dimensional normed space has a sequence of unit vectors whose pairwise distances exceed 1/21/2. To construct the next vector, let LL be the span of the finitely many previous ones. This finite-dimensional subspace is closed and is proper. Choose y∉Ly\notin L, put d=dist⁡(y,L)>0d=\operatorname{dist}(y,L)>0, and choose l∈Ll\in L with ∥y−l∥<2d\|y-l\|<2d. Then x=(y−l)/∥y−l∥x=(y-l)/\|y-l\| has norm one and distance d/∥y−l∥>1/2d/\|y-l\|>1/2 from LL. Induction gives the asserted sequence, which cannot have a Cauchy subsequence. Applying this to FF would contradict compactness of BFB_F. Hence FF is finite-dimensional, and its subspace MM satisfies

dim⁡M<∞.(GF65) \dim M<\infty. \tag{GF65}

Apply this once to M=ker⁡AmM=\ker A_m through (GF54), and once to the range annihilator through the compact transpose identity (GF54D).

13. Reading notes and references

The mixed symbol and Sobolev estimates used here are proved in the four named prerequisite lessons at the start. The residue projection and its stable Cauchy range come from Cauchy data from jumps and residues, while the order reductions, boundary source, exterior-jet construction, and functional-analytic index argument extend the corresponding differential proofs in Solving an elliptic system from compatible boundary measurements.

A related primary source with author-submitted TeX is Gerd Grubb, “Fractional Laplacians on domains, a development of Hörmander’s theory of μ-transmission pseudodifferential operators,” arXiv:1310.0951v5. The present lesson gives its own proofs of (GF1)–(GF65) and does not use either reference as a replacement for a displayed argument.

The remaining sections provide the complete collar, normal expansion, half-space, source, trace and freezing proofs used above. Section 23 records the exact correction of the stronger local estimate; Section 24 supplies the full principal-symbol comparison and the globally scoped dual relation.

14. Patching the original collar operator with both error bundles

The unchanged collar object and its two weights

Let XX be compact with smooth boundary YY, and fix one collar c:Y×[0,ϵ)→Xc:Y\times[0,\epsilon)\to X with inward coordinate r≥0r\geq0. Fix the source and target bundles E,FE,F, their collar identifications with the pullbacks of EY,FYE_Y,F_Y, and Hermitian norms. Write Dr=−i∂rD_r=-i\partial_r. The operator in the collar is Pb=∑j=0mAj(r)Drj:EY→FY,Aj(r)∈Ψphgm−j(Y;EY,FY),Am(r)=M(r),(GI1) P^b=\sum_{j=0}^{m}A_j(r)D_r^j:E_Y\longrightarrow F_Y, \qquad A_j(r)\in\Psi_{\mathrm{phg}}^{m-j}(Y;E_Y,F_Y), \qquad A_m(r)=M(r), \tag{GI1} where m≥1m\geq1, M(r)M(r) is a bundle map, the families are smooth in r∈(−1,1)r\in(-1,1), and they vanish for r>2/3r>2/3 in this original collar presentation. The interior term Pi∈Ψphgm(X∘;E,F)P^i\in\Psi_{\mathrm{phg}}^m(X^\circ;E,F) has kernel supported in (X\X1/2)2(X\setminus X_{1/2})^2. Thus P=Pb+PiP=P^b+P^i equals PbP^b when either operator variable is in a sufficiently narrow collar. The interior term and the extension of (GI1) away from that narrow collar are retained as parts of the original object; the construction below only uses the region where (GI1) actually represents PP.

The original boundary operators are also retained: Bju=∑k=0m−1Bjkγku,γku=(Drku)|r=0,Bjk∈Ψphgmj−k(Y;EY,Gj).(GI1a) B_j u=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}B_{jk}\gamma_k u, \quad \gamma_k u=(D_r^ku)|_{r=0}, \quad B_{jk}\in\Psi_{\mathrm{phg}}^{m_j-k}(Y;E_Y,G_j). \tag{GI1a} Their transverse degree is below mm, while the total order mjm_j is unrestricted. They play no role in inverting PcP_c on the full cylinder, but their exact transformation and trace targets are recorded in GI-007; a boundary condition is never inferred from the interior inverse alone.

In every chart of YY, put x=(y,r)x=(y,r), ξ=(η,κ)\xi=(\eta,\kappa), and R(η,κ)=1+|(η,κ)|,T(η)=1+|η|.(GI2) R(\eta,\kappa)=1+|(\eta,\kappa)|,\qquad T(\eta)=1+|\eta|. \tag{GI2} The local mixed class Sa,bS^{a,b} has all seminorms supx,η,κ∥∂xβ∂ηγ∂κℓa(x,η,κ)∥Ra−ℓTb−|γ|<∞.(GI3) \sup_{x,\eta,\kappa} \frac{\|\partial_x^\beta\partial_\eta^\gamma\partial_\kappa^\ell a(x,\eta,\kappa)\|} {R^{a-\ell}T^{b-|\gamma|}}<\infty. \tag{GI3} The total-frequency order and tangential order are different. The Sobolev Hilbert norm instead has the smooth quadratic multipliers ∥u∥H(s,t)2=(2π)−dim⁡X∫(1+|ξ|2)s(1+|η|2)t∥û(ξ)∥2dξ.(GI4) \|u\|_{H_{(s,t)}}^2=(2\pi)^{-\dim X}\int (1+|\xi|^2)^s(1+|\eta|^2)^t\|\widehat u(\xi)\|^2\,d\xi. \tag{GI4} The mixed inverse and mixed Sobolev prerequisite lessons prove the exact identity of the vectors and equivalent seminorms/norms obtained from (GI2) and the corresponding square-root quadratic weights. The factors in (GI2) and (GI4) are never identified numerically.

For the gluing argument let ℳa\mathscr M^a denote the proper fixed-collar operators defined exactly in GI-003a below: they have local symbols Sa,0S^{a,0} in common tangential charts and retain tangentially separated normal kernels of order aa. Let ℰa⊂ℳa\mathscr E^a\subset\mathscr M^a denote the enhanced operators whose local symbols satisfy ∂ξka∈Sa−1,0(1≤k≤dim⁡X).(GI5) \partial_{\xi_k}a\in S^{a-1,0}\quad(1\leq k\leq\dim X). \tag{GI5} The enhanced class also has tangentially separated normal kernels one total order lower, as GI-003a proves. A smooth kernel of compact support is in every ℳa,b\mathscr M^{a,b}, but a tangentially smoothing operator followed by DrjD_r^j need not have a smooth full kernel.

Shrink to a closed interval I=[−δ,δ]⊂(−1,1)I=[-\delta,\delta]\subset(-1,1) so that the extension of (GI1) remains elliptic and M(y,r):Ey→FyM(y,r):E_y\to F_y is invertible on Y×IY\times I. Tangentially separated kernels and the global product class

For any real aa, define a normal residual kernel of order aa, on a compact pair of tangential chart pieces, by the oscillatory expression K(y,r;z,s)=(2π)−1Os⁡∫ei(r−s)κk(y,z,r,s,κ)dκ,∥∂y,z,r,sβ∂κℓk∥≤Cβℓ(1+|κ|)a−ℓ.(GI19a) K(y,r;z,s)=(2\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{Os}\int e^{i(r-s)\kappa}k(y,z,r,s,\kappa)\,d\kappa, \quad \|\partial_{y,z,r,s}^{\beta}\partial_\kappa^\ell k\| \leq C_{\beta\ell}(1+|\kappa|)^{a-\ell}. \tag{GI19a} The amplitude is smooth in both independent tangential variables, including between different tangential charts, and carries the actual F⊠E*⊗ΩinputF\boxtimes E^*\otimes\Omega_{\rm input} kernel factors. Denote this class by 𝒩a\mathcal N^a. For the cylinder operators constructed below, the displayed constants are uniform in all r,sr,s on the proper normal support |r−s|≤L|r-s|\leq L; on the original finite collar, compact-local constants suffice. A change (GI14) acts on y,zy,z by the smooth diffeomorphisms ϕr,ϕs\phi_r,\phi_s and leaves the phase (r-s) intact, so the estimates and density factors in (GI19a) are preserved on compact normal strips. The actual cylinder atlas uses the rr-independent pullback charts, making the bounds uniform on its entire normal line. Normal amplitude reduction proves that replacing k(y,z,r,s,κ)k(y,z,r,s,\kappa) by a left normal symbol does not change the class. If r≠sr\ne s, arbitrarily many normal integrations by parts make this kernel smooth; if only y≠zy\ne z, it may stay singular, as (GI19) shows.

One precise local characterization is useful. With compact cutoffs in y,z,r,sy,z,r,s, a kernel has the form (GI19a) if and only if its left symbol belongs to Sa,bS^{a,b} for every real bb. For the forward direction, Fourier transform the smooth tangential kernel in (y-z); integrating by parts in zz arbitrarily often gives T−L(1+|κ|)a−ℓT^{-L}(1+|\kappa|)^{a-\ell}, with any LL. The exact inequalities 1+|κ|≤R≤(1+|κ|)T(GI19b) 1+|\kappa|\leq R\leq(1+|\kappa|)T \tag{GI19b} transfer this to Ra−ℓTb−|γ|R^{a-\ell}T^{b-|\gamma|} for every prescribed b,γ,ℓb,\gamma,\ell, choosing LL after those indices. For the reverse direction, partially invert the tangential Fourier transform; each desired y,zy,z derivative inserts a finite power of η\eta, and choosing bb sufficiently negative makes that power and the required normal-frequency derivative integrable. Equation (GI19b) then bounds the result by (1+|κ|)a−ℓ(1+|\kappa|)^{a-\ell}. Normal amplitude reduction handles separate r,sr,s dependence. These two calculations retain every differentiated seminorm.

If a compactly localized left symbol a∈Sq,0a\in S^{q,0} is cut to y≠zy\ne z, integrate its tangential Fourier kernel by parts LL times with ei(y−z)η=((y−z)⋅∂η)/(i|y−z|2)ei(y−z)ηe^{i(y-z)\eta}=((y-z)\cdot\partial_\eta)/(i|y-z|^2)e^{i(y-z)\eta}. The differentiated amplitude is Rq−ℓT−LR^{q-\ell}T^{-L}, so the resulting kernel is in 𝒩q\mathcal N^q by (GI19b). If a∈ℰqa\in\mathscr E^q, take the first tangential derivative using its strengthened Sq−1,0S^{q-1,0} estimate, then take (L-1) further tangential derivatives. The result is 𝒩q−1\mathcal N^{q-1}. Derivatives of the separation denominator cost finite extra tangential powers and are absorbed by choosing LL larger. This proves the exact off-diagonal order claimed in GI-003; it does not turn the piece into a smooth full kernel.

We can now finish the definition used throughout. An operator belongs to ℳq\mathscr M^q when each compact localization with both tangential variables in one chart has a left symbol Sq,0S^{q,0}, and its tangentially separated kernel is locally 𝒩q\mathcal N^q. It belongs to ℰq\mathscr E^q when the local symbols have (GI5) and the separated kernel is 𝒩q−1\mathcal N^{q-1}. The preceding calculations and GI-003 prove independence of the product chart and frame. They also give the inclusions ℳq−1⊂ℰq⊂ℳq\mathscr M^{q-1}\subset\mathscr E^q\subset\mathscr M^q.

The two composition facts used later follow with no loss of a separated normal term: ℳaℳb⊂ℳa+b,ℳa𝒩b,𝒩bℳa⊂𝒩a+b,(GI19c) \mathscr M^a\mathscr M^b\subset\mathscr M^{a+b}, \qquad \mathscr M^a\mathcal N^b,\ \mathcal N^b\mathscr M^a \subset\mathcal N^{a+b}, \tag{GI19c} for proper operators. In a common tangential chart the first assertion is the mixed composition theorem. For a separated factor, its symbol has every second order (b’), by the characterization above; compose it by the mixed composition theorem with the regular Sa,0S^{a,0} symbol to obtain every Sa+b,b′S^{a+b,b'}, then return by the same characterization to 𝒩a+b\mathcal N^{a+b}. A finite partition in the intermediate tangential variable reduces the remaining configurations to these two cases: if external tangential points are separated, at least one factor is separated after sufficiently small intermediate pieces. Proper support confines the intermediate variables to a compact set, so only finitely many pieces occur on each localization. This proves (GI19c) on actual kernels, including their input densities.

For a scalar cutoff ff, the local commutator calculation in (GI25) shows [A,f]∈ℳq−1[A,f]\in\mathscr M^{q-1} when A∈ℰqA\in\mathscr E^q. Away from the tangential diagonal, its kernel is multiplied by (fz,sz,s-fy,ry,r) and still has normal residual order (q-1). Thus this commutator statement is valid globally. The actual PcP_c is in ℰm\mathscr E^m: its top normal coefficient is a bundle-map multiplication kernel on the tangential diagonal, and the off-diagonal kernels of its lower coefficients have normal degree at most (m-1). Each TiT_i is in ℰ−m\mathscr E^{-m} after localization, by its enhanced derivative bounds and the separated-kernel calculation. These facts justify every global class membership and composition in GI-004–GI-006.

The exact overlap inverse and bundle maps

In a common chart, write pi:Ei→Fip_i:E_i\to F_i for the local symbol of PcP_c. Transport the symbol from chart jj with the actual two bundle transfers as in (GI17), and write it p̃j\widetilde p_j. Choose a common exterior frequency region where both actual matrices are invertible. The pointwise inverse identity, with its indispensable matrix order, is pi−1−p̃j−1=pi−1(p̃j−pi)p̃j−1∈S−m−1,0(Fi,Ei).(GI21) p_i^{-1}-\widetilde p_j^{-1} =p_i^{-1}(\widetilde p_j-p_i)\widetilde p_j^{-1} \in S^{-m-1,0}(F_i,E_i). \tag{GI21} The first factor is Fi→EiF_i\to E_i, the middle factor Ei→FiE_i\to F_i, and the last factor Fi→EiF_i\to E_i, read right to left. Both exterior inverses are S−m,0S^{-m,0} by the mixed inverse theorem. Their frequency cutoffs may be enlarged to a common one; the difference between two permissible cutoffs has compact frequency support and belongs to every Sa,bS^{a,b}. Equation (GI17) for the enhanced τ symbols then proves that the operators transported between charts satisfy Ti−UijETj(UijF)−1∈ℳ−m−1(GI22) T_i-U^E_{ij}T_j(U^F_{ij})^{-1} \in\mathscr M^{-m-1} \tag{GI22} after compact overlap localization. This is the precise overlap map; it does not identify EE with FF outside the collar. The two ordered errors themselves transport only as members of ℳ−1\mathscr M^{-1}, which is exactly the order required in the patching calculation.

There is a second proof of the order in (GI22) that exposes the relation between the two error sides. In any one chart where two properly localized approximate inverses S,T:F→ES,T:F\to E obey SP=IE+LESP=I_E+L_E and PT=IF+RFPT=I_F+R_F, associativity gives the exact identity S−T=LET−SRF.(GI23) S-T=L_ET-SR_F. \tag{GI23} Its two products have the indicated order S−1,0∘S−m,0=S−m−1,0S^{-1,0}\circ S^{-m,0}=S^{-m-1,0}. The order of the factors and the (E/F) subscripts are forced by their domains and codomains. Formula (GI21) proves the corresponding pointwise statement, while (GI23) proves uniqueness of a two-sided operator inverse modulo one lower total order. The word “unique” here refers to this quotient, not to a canonical lower-order full symbol.

A global cylinder inverse with both ordered errors

Left multiplication by ϑi\vartheta_i is direct. The same exact kernel multiplication by ϑi(y)ϑi(z)\vartheta_i(y)\vartheta_i(z) preserves (AL9). The preferred chart/frame changes depend on yy, not on rr, so their exact kernel transports do not mix the two normal tails. At leading normal order, each local ci0=Mi−1c_{i0}=M_i^{-1} is a bundle-map multiplication symbol. 17. The full paired normal class and its finite products

A paired real-normal class with its original weights

Work in the preferred rr-independent pullback charts of the fixed collar. Let a∈ℤa\in\mathbb Z. A normally proper operator AA belongs to ℒa(FY,EY)\mathcal L^a(F_Y,E_Y) when it belongs to the actual global mixed class ℳa\mathscr M^a of GI19a–GI19c and has these two additional properties, with all source/target bundles and input densities retained.

On every compact localization in a common tangential chart, its exact left symbol 𝔞(y,r,η,κ)\mathfrak a(y,r,\eta,\kappa) has one sequence of complete tangential-operator coefficients An(r)∈Ψtann(FY,EY)A_n(r)\in\Psi_{\rm tan}^n(F_Y,E_Y). If an(y,r,η)a_n(y,r,\eta) is their complete left symbol, then, on |κ|≥CT(η)|\kappa|\geq C T(\eta), for every L≥1L\geq1, every base derivative β\beta, tangential frequency derivative α\alpha, and normal frequency derivative vv, ∥∂y,rβ∂ηα∂κv(𝔞−∑n=0L−1anκa−n)∥≤CLαβv|κ|a−L−vTL−|α|.(AC1) \left\|\partial_{y,r}^{\beta}\partial_\eta^\alpha\partial_\kappa^v \left(\mathfrak a-\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}a_n\kappa^{a-n}\right)\right\| \leq C_{L\alpha\beta v}|\kappa|^{a-L-v}T^{L-|\alpha|}. \tag{AC1} The coefficients and constants may be transported between preferred charts by the actual rr-independent bundle maps. In the other preferred chart, the coefficient is the exact conjugated tangential operator, not a guessed pointwise symbol. The same sequence is used for positive and negative κ\kappa.

For disjoint compact tangential output/input cutoffs, the normal amplitude of the actual kernel has an expansion by the off-diagonal smooth kernels of these same AnA_n, after the actual normal properness cutoff, and |∂y,z,r,sγ∂κv(kA−∑n=0L−1kA,nκa−n)|≤CγLv|κ|a−L−v(AC2) \left|\partial_{y,z,r,s}^{\gamma}\partial_\kappa^v \left(k_A-\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}k_{A,n}\kappa^{a-n}\right)\right| \leq C_{\gamma Lv}|\kappa|^{a-L-v} \tag{AC2} on every compact proper normal strip. Here the amplitude is reduced to the left normal symbol near r=sr=s; a normally proper cutoff is inserted after that reduction and equals one there. Changing this cutoff changes the localized kernel by a compact smooth full kernel, hence changes its normal amplitude by a rapidly decreasing function of |κ||\kappa|. The coefficient kernels are the actual off-diagonal kernels of An(r)A_n(r), multiplied by that cutoff and by the input density and local frame factors; those factors are differentiated in γ\gamma. Equations (AC1)–(AC2) are required at every length, not only for the leading principal symbol. A compact smooth full kernel belongs to every ℒa\mathcal L^a with every coefficient zero.

The obvious filtration is exact: ℒa−1⊂ℒa\mathcal L^{a-1}\subset\mathcal L^a. To see the coefficient assertion, insert a zero leading coefficient and shift AnA_n to index n+1n+1. Its tangential order nn is at most n+1n+1; the remainder inequality follows from T≥1T\geq1, and the separated-kernel inequality follows from the corresponding one-power shift. This inclusion does not identify the two different orders RR and TT.

Exact composition and its full coefficient formula

For composable A∈ℒa(F,E)A\in\mathcal L^a(F,E) and B∈ℒb(G,F)B\in\mathcal L^b(G,F), their actual proper composition belongs to ℒa+b(G,E)\mathcal L^{a+b}(G,E). Its order is at most p+q≤np+q\leq n. Equation (AC3) is NL3 with its coefficients realized as actual operators; it does not commute any of the displayed factors.

Here is a proof of both remainder assertions. Tangentially, the exact left-symbol product of the two parameter families is the oscillatory integral used in MC2–MC20. For a compact localization, split its tangential frequency shift ζ\zeta at |ζ|=ε|κ||\zeta|=\varepsilon|\kappa|. In the smaller region, choose the output cone constant large enough that both shifted and unshifted frequencies lie in the cones of (AC1). Insert both length-LL expansions. Every term with p+q≥Lp+q\geq L is bounded by C|κ|a+b−L−vTL−|α|(AC4) C|\kappa|^{a+b-L-v}T^{L-|\alpha|} \tag{AC4} after any requested derivatives: use T(η+ζ)≤T(η)(1+|ζ|)T(\eta+\zeta)\leq T(\eta)(1+|\zeta|), its reverse inequality, and T/|κ|≤C−1T/|\kappa|\leq C^{-1} to absorb the excess p+q−Lp+q-L. The exact tangential composition of a term with p+q<Lp+q<L is ApBqA_pB_q, with no truncation of its tangential symbol. A remainder factor satisfies (AC4) by (AC1) and the finite-seminorm oscillatory estimate (MC6) applied to the shifted orders; the polynomial moment of the compact base cutoff absorbs the Peetre factor. In the larger shift region, integrate by parts NN times in the compact tangential base difference. Each differentiation falls on a smooth compact cutoff or a symbol with the GI3 bounds, while the transformed cutoff is O((1+|ζ|)−N)O((1+|\zeta|)^{-N}). For any prescribed decay exponent MM, take NN beyond the GI3 polynomial growth order, the tangential dimension, every requested derivative order, and MM. The resulting integral is O(|κ|−M)O(|\kappa|^{-M}). This establishes tangential composition of the complete coefficients and the differentiated cone remainder.

For the normal variable, the exact normally proper composition is the operator-valued oscillatory integral (AL16): (A∘B)(r,κ)=(2π)−1Os⁡∫e−itλA(r,κ+λ)B(r+t,κ)dtdλ.(AC5) (A\circ B)(r,\kappa)=(2\pi)^{-1}\operatorname{Os} \int e^{-it\lambda}A(r,\kappa+\lambda)\,B(r+t,\kappa)\,dt\,d\lambda . \tag{AC5} The product inside is the exact tangential composition just controlled. The normal support in tt is compact after localization. Split at |λ|=ε|κ||\lambda|=\varepsilon|\kappa|, decreasing ε\varepsilon so the small region stays in the high-normal cones. On the small region, Taylor-expand A(r,κ+λ)A(r,\kappa+\lambda) in λ\lambda to the finite order needed for the requested length LL. The identity λℓe−itλ=iℓ∂tℓe−itλ\lambda^\ell e^{-it\lambda}=i^\ell\partial_t^\ell e^{-it\lambda}, followed by integration by parts in tt, gives the full moment, after restoring the complementary frequency region by NC5 in Section 18, ∂κℓAδℓB/ℓ!\partial_\kappa^\ell A\,\delta^\ell B/\ell! at t=0t=0. Since ∂κℓ(apκa−p)/ℓ!=(a−pℓ)apκa−p−ℓ\partial_\kappa^\ell(a_p\kappa^{a-p})/\ell!=\binom{a-p}{\ell}a_p\kappa^{a-p-\ell}, the coefficient at total index n=p+q+ℓn=p+q+\ell is exactly (AC3).

For the integral Taylor remainder of length LL, integrate its factor λL\lambda^L by parts LL times in tt. The resulting ∂κLA(r,κ+θλ)δLB(r+t,κ)\partial_\kappa^L A(r,\kappa+\theta\lambda)\,\delta^L B(r+t,\kappa) has the bound (AC4), with arbitrary requested additional derivatives, because ∂κL\partial_\kappa^L contributes |κ|−L|\kappa|^{-L} and each normal base derivative preserves the tangential order. Apply the finite-seminorm oscillatory bound of MC6 in the remaining compact t,λt,\lambda variables, with N>2L+|α|+|β|+v+|a|+|b|+3N>2L+|\alpha|+|\beta|+v+|a|+|b|+3 integrations by parts to make its absolute majorant integrable. Derivatives of the small-region cutoff lie where |λ|≍|κ||\lambda|\asymp|\kappa| and have an extra |κ|−1|\kappa|^{-1} for each normal-frequency derivative. On |λ|≥ε|κ||\lambda|\geq\varepsilon|\kappa|, integrate by parts NN times in tt; the NN-th tt derivative of the compactly supported BB amplitude obeys the same GI3 polynomial bounds, while |λ|−N|\lambda|^{-N} makes the λ\lambda-integral O(|κ|−M)O(|\kappa|^{-M}) for any prescribed MM after increasing NN. This includes the region where κ+λ\kappa+\lambda crosses zero, so no false high-normal expansion is used there. The normal properness cutoffs equal one when each normal input-output difference is near zero. Their omitted pieces have compact smooth full kernels there: if an intermediate normal point is away from the output and the final input tends to the output, both proper factors are away from their own normal diagonals. Repeated normal-frequency integration by parts makes those pieces rapidly decreasing in the output normal symbol. Thus the coefficients calculated at t=0t=0 are the actual coefficients modulo a rapid normal remainder. These estimates prove (AC1) for the product at every length and preserve its common coefficients on both signs of κ\kappa.

For (AC2), fix disjoint external tangential cutoffs and partition the compact intermediate tangential variable into finitely many sufficiently small supports. For each intermediate piece, either the first factor is tangentially separated from the output or the second is separated from the input. In the first case the kernel of AA is smooth in both tangential variables and has (AC2); its partial tangential Fourier transform has every negative TT-order after integration by parts in its smooth input variable, exactly as in the forward implication GI19b. Compose it with the complete symbol of BB. Its high tangential-frequency part is O(|κ|−M)O(|\kappa|^{-M}) for any MM: choose the negative TT-order beyond M+dM+d and use T≳|κ|T\gtrsim|\kappa| there. Its low part obeys (AC4) and the normal calculation (AC5), with each external tangential derivative absorbed by choosing the smoothing order further below −d-d. The other case reverses A,BA,B and uses the same estimates. The coefficient kernel obtained by the finite intermediate integral is exactly the off-diagonal kernel of (AC3), including the input density. The normal remainder is O(|κ|a+b−L−v)O(|\kappa|^{a+b-L-v}) with all external derivatives. This proves (AC2) and actual closure under proper composition, rather than merely diagonal symbol closure.

Differential factors, local errors, and the two global errors

The original cylinder polynomial Pc=∑j=0mAj(r)Drj:EY→FYP_c=\sum_{j=0}^mA_j(r)D_r^j:E_Y\to F_Y belongs to ℒm\mathcal L^m. These statements are identities, so both (AC1) and the off-diagonal normal polynomial in (AC2) have zero remainder after length m+1m+1. The original top coefficient Am=MA_m=M is a bundle-map multiplication operator; it is not replaced by II. The actual local TiT_i and patched QQ belong to ℒ−m\mathcal L^{-m} by AL1–AL13. Their leading coefficients are Mi−1M_i^{-1} and M−1M^{-1}, respectively.

One more exact gain is needed before reindexing an error from degree zero to degree −1-1. For a local pip_i or τi\tau_i, the leading coefficient MiM_i or Mi−1M_i^{-1} is independent of η\eta. Consequently ∂κpi∈ℒm−1\partial_\kappa p_i\in\mathcal L^{m-1}, ∂ηpi∈ℒm−1\partial_\eta p_i\in\mathcal L^{m-1}, ∂κτi∈ℒ−m−1\partial_\kappa\tau_i\in\mathcal L^{-m-1}, and ∂ητi∈ℒ−m−1\partial_\eta\tau_i\in\mathcal L^{-m-1}, with each tangential derivative interpreted componentwise. For ∂κ\partial_\kappa, this follows directly by differentiating (AC1) and (AC2), lowering every normal power by one. For ∂η\partial_\eta, the index-zero term vanishes; a term at old index n≥1n\geq1 has tangential order at most n−1n-1 after differentiation and is the new index n−1n-1. The differentiated remainder has the required new bound because its TT-power falls by one. On a separated kernel, ∂η\partial_\eta corresponds to multiplication by the exact tangential difference, and the vanishing leading multiplication kernel produces the same shift. These facts also apply to PcP_c and QQ, since their leading coefficients are M,M−1M,M^{-1}.

In a local chart the pointwise matrix product piτi=θiIFp_i\tau_i=\theta_i I_F, and θi−IF\theta_i-I_F has compact support in the full frequency variables. Its quantization has a smooth full kernel and lies in every ℒa\mathcal L^a. At least one frequency derivative falls on pip_i; the preceding gain places that derivative in ℒm−1\mathcal L^{m-1}, while the differentiated τi\tau_i stays in ℒ−m\mathcal L^{-m}. For clarity about that parameter step, MC21 replaces the second base argument in (AC5) by r+tur+t u, and the tangential base argument by the same scaled shift, for 0≤t≤10\leq t\leq1. The two frequency-shift splits above remain valid uniformly in tt: derivatives of B(r+tu)B(r+t u) acquire factors tj≤1t^j\leq1, and neither cone condition nor any integrable majorant changes. The exact identities themselves remain the two distinct GI32 sides: PcQN=IF−(−ℛF)N,QNPc=IE−(−ℛE)N.(AC9) P_cQ_N=I_F-(-\mathcal R_F)^N,\qquad Q_NP_c=I_E-(-\mathcal R_E)^N . \tag{AC9} Equations (AC1)–(AC9) establish the analytic common-tail and tangentially separated kernel closure that was missing in NK5 for the actual finite patched operators. They do not, by themselves, evaluate the one-sided normal Fourier limit of QNPcQ_NP^c, prove its weighted remainder at every original mjm_j, or compare the differential interior freezing TT with T0T_0. Those are separate calculations: the full original source SR12a must be inserted into the now-proved expansion, its polynomial normal pieces must be treated as boundary-supported distributions rather than assigned point values, and both AC9 error sides must remain present.

The separate boundary calculation has now been carried out in AT1–AT15. It uses, rather than silently includes within AC1–AC9, the full source SR12a and the upper normal integral T16. The separate comparison is proved in Section 22.

18. Exact composition moments and differentiated remainders

1. The exact tangential product, with no tangential truncation

Let A∈ℒa(F,E)A\in\mathcal L^a(F,E) and B∈ℒb(G,F)B\in\mathcal L^b(G,F), for integers a,ba,b, in the original preferred product charts. 3. Both separated-kernel configurations and the literal finite inverse

For disjoint external tangential supports, cover the compact intermediate tangential set by finitely many small pieces. On each piece either the first kernel is separated from the output or the second is separated from the input. A separated coefficient kernel is smooth in both tangential variables; partial tangential Fourier transformation and arbitrary integration by parts give every negative TT-order. The AC2 remainder at length LL has the same property, with original normal power |κ|a−L−v|\kappa|^{a-L-v} or |κ|b−L−v|\kappa|^{b-L-v}.

In the smaller tangential frequency region T≤C|κ|T\leq C|\kappa|, choose the negative tangential order below minus the tangential dimension, the polynomial growth orders of the other factor, and all requested external derivative costs. The tangential integral is then absolutely convergent with the normal remainder |κ|a+b−L−v|\kappa|^{a+b-L-v}. On T≥C|κ|T\geq C|\kappa|, choose the negative order further below any prescribed decay exponent; integrating its tail makes the contribution arbitrarily rapid in |κ||\kappa|. Apply the exact normal calculation (NC3)–(NC6) to these amplitudes. It gives the same normal remainder and the off-diagonal kernel of the complete coefficient in (NC6).

This argument works in either factor order: when the first factor is separated, transform its smooth input variable; when the second is separated, transform its smooth output variable and retain the transposed pairing in its original order. No factor is commuted. Finite intermediate integration and the original input density give the actual composed kernel. Away from the normal diagonal repeated normal frequency integration makes all omitted properness pieces smooth in all variables; on the normal diagonal the separated singularities and their coefficients remain present.

For the actual polynomial, its leading coefficient is the original bundle map MM, and the actual inverse seed has leading coefficient M−1M^{-1}. Differentiating their expansions in a tangential frequency kills the leading multiplication symbol. The old index n≥1n\geq1 has tangential order reduced from nn to n−1n-1, allowing reindexing into one lower normal class. A normal frequency derivative reduces every normal power by one. The original enhanced GI5 bounds give the same improvement globally, not only on the exterior cone. The scaled base shifts have factors between zero and one; the preceding compact Fourier majorants are uniform in that scale, so the remainder belongs to ℒ−1\mathcal L^{-1} at every coefficient. Use the original mixed norm ∥w∥(s,t)2=(2π)−n∫ℝn−1∫ℝ(1+|η|2+ζ2)s(1+|η|2)t|ŵ(η,ζ)|2dζdη.(SR12c) \|w\|_{(s,t)}^2=(2\pi)^{-n} \int_{\mathbb R^{n-1}}\int_{\mathbb R} (1+|\eta|^2+\zeta^2)^s(1+|\eta|^2)^t |\widehat w(\eta,\zeta)|^2\,d\zeta\,d\eta. \tag{SR12c} For 0≤b<m0\leq b<m, direct normal-frequency integration, with no change of the original tangential weight, gives ∥v⊗Drbδ0∥(−m,T)2=B(b+12,m−b−12)2π∥v∥HT−m+b+1/2(Y)2.(SR12d) \|v\otimes D_r^b\delta_0\|_{(-m,T)}^2 =\frac{B(b+\tfrac12,m-b-\tfrac12)}{2\pi} \|v\|_{H^{T-m+b+1/2}(Y)}^2. \tag{SR12d} Indeed, writing h=(1+|η|2)1/2h=(1+|\eta|^2)^{1/2}, the normal integral is ∫ℝζ2b(h2+ζ2)−mdζ=h2b+1−2mB(b+12,m−b−12)\int_{\mathbb R}\zeta^{2b}(h^2+\zeta^2)^{-m}\,d\zeta =h^{2b+1-2m}B(b+\tfrac12,m-b-\tfrac12). It is finite since b≤m−1b\leq m-1. In the term of (SR6) indexed by (ℓ,k,q)(\ell,k,q), set a=ℓ−1−ka=\ell-1-k, b=k−qb=k-q. Its coefficient belongs to HT−a−1/2−(m−ℓ)=HT−m+b+q+1/2(Y;F).(SR12e) H^{T-a-1/2-(m-\ell)} =H^{T-m+b+q+1/2}(Y;F). \tag{SR12e} The q=0q=0 terms therefore have the regularity needed by (SR12d). Every defect term has q≥1q\geq1, so it has at least one further tangential order. The finite sum and (SR12d) prove the actual bounded maps CP:𝒰T→H(−m,T)(Y×ℝ;F),Δc:𝒰T→H(−m,T+1)(Y×ℝ;F).(SR12f) C_P:\mathcal U_T\longrightarrow H_{(-m,T)}(Y\times\mathbb R;F), \qquad \Delta^c:\mathcal U_T\longrightarrow H_{(-m,T+1)}(Y\times\mathbb R;F). \tag{SR12f} The latter gain is a statement about the supported source, not yet about QCPQ C_P or its boundary trace.

For jets supplied by a positive-side section, the exact flat Fourier trace estimate gives, when s>a+1/2s>a+1/2, ∥γau∥Hs+t−a−1/2(Y)≤[B(a+12,s−a−12)2π]1/2∥u∥(s,t);+.(SR12g) \|\gamma_a u\|_{H^{s+t-a-1/2}(Y)} \leq \left[\frac{B(a+\tfrac12,s-a-\tfrac12)}{2\pi}\right]^{1/2} \|u\|_{(s,t);+}. \tag{SR12g} For a whole-space extension this follows by Fourier inversion at r=0r=0, Cauchy–Schwarz in ζ\zeta, and ∫ℝζ2a(h2+ζ2)−sdζ=h2a+1−2sB(a+12,s−a−12)\int_{\mathbb R}\zeta^{2a}(h^2+\zeta^2)^{-s}\,d\zeta =h^{2a+1-2s}B(a+\tfrac12,s-a-\tfrac12). The one-sided value is independent of the extension because the difference of two extensions vanishes for r>0r>0 and has a continuous aa-th trace at this exponent. Taking the infimum over extensions proves (SR12g) for the restriction norm. Consequently (SR12f) applies to all jets of u∈H(s,t)(ℝ+n;E)u\in H_{(s,t)}(\mathbb R_+^n;E) if s>m−1/2s>m-1/2, with T=s+tT=s+t. No trace below this threshold follows from this proof. On a compact boundary, the mapping statement follows chart by chart with equivalent norms; the beta constants in (SR12d) and (SR12g) belong to the stated flat norm.

Exact parametrix morphism with both error sides

The source defect also enters the operator comparison. Keep actual bundle domains: P,P0:E→FP,P_0:E\to F, Q,Q0:F→EQ,Q_0:F\to E. On a common test/distribution domain where the properly supported products act, write their distinct approximate identities as Q0P0=IE+RE,0,PQ=IF+RF.(SR13) Q_0P_0=I_E+R_{E,0},\qquad PQ=I_F+R_F. \tag{SR13} Expanding the ordered product Q0(P0−P)QQ_0(P_0-P)Q, without commuting factors, proves Q−Q0=Q0(P0−P)Q−RE,0Q+Q0RF.(SR14) \boxed{\displaystyle Q-Q_0=Q_0(P_0-P)Q-R_{E,0}Q+Q_0R_F.} \tag{SR14} Indeed its first two factors give (IE+RE,0)Q(I_E+R_{E,0})Q, and its second pair gives Q0(IF+RF)Q_0(I_F+R_F); solving the resulting exact equality yields (SR14). The remainders act on different bundles and are not identified.

Set L=QCPL=QC_P, L0=Q0C0L_0=Q_0C_0, as actual maps from the original boundary jets to EE-valued distributions. Adding and subtracting Q0CPQ_0C_P, then inserting (SR14), gives the exact layer morphism L−L0=Q0(P0−P)L−RE,0L+Q0RFCP+Q0Δc.(SR15) \boxed{\displaystyle L-L_0 =Q_0(P_0-P)L-R_{E,0}L+Q_0R_FC_P+Q_0\Delta^c.} \tag{SR15} The final term is the source change (SR6). It survives even if the interior inverses were exact. No boundary trace is applied to (SR15) until the relevant trace mapping is proved; this avoids turning a distributional identity into an unsupported Calderón estimate. In the explicit cylinder below all kernels and traces exist, so the trace of (SR15) can be calculated.

This boundary-supported change differs from applying P0P_0 to the original zero extension while retaining the original interior equation. The exact latter identity is P0(u0)−(Pu)0=C0U+1r>0∑ℓ=0m(Aℓ(0)−Aℓ(r))Drℓu.(SR15a) P_0(u^0)-(Pu)^0 =C_0U+1_{r>0}\sum_{\ell=0}^{m} \bigl(A_\ell(0)-A_\ell(r)\bigr)D_r^\ell u. \tag{SR15a} It follows by adding and subtracting (P0u)0(P_0u)^0. Its second summand is an interior defect; it cannot be counted as part of the supported map Δc\Delta^c.

20. Half-space mapping and the entire supported-source norm

1. The original class and the maps to be proved

In a preferred product chart with tangential dimension dd, retain R(η,κ)=1+|(η,κ)|,T(η)=1+|η|,λ(η)=(1+|η|2)1/2,Q(η,κ)=(1+|η|2+κ2)1/2.(MH1) R(\eta,\kappa)=1+|(\eta,\kappa)|, \qquad T(\eta)=1+|\eta|, \qquad \lambda(\eta)=(1+|\eta|^2)^{1/2}, \qquad Q(\eta,\kappa)=(1+|\eta|^2+\kappa^2)^{1/2}. \tag{MH1} Here R,TR,T are the original symbol weights and Q,λQ,\lambda are the original quadratic Sobolev weights. In particular Q2=λ2+κ2Q^2=\lambda^2+\kappa^2, Q≥λQ\geq\lambda, λ≤T≤2λ\lambda\leq T\leq\sqrt2\lambda, and Q≤R≤2QQ\leq R\leq\sqrt2Q. These inequalities prove comparison; none is a numerical identification of the weights.

Let A:FY→EYA:F_Y\to E_Y belong to the actual normally proper class ℒa\mathcal L^a, for an integer aa. Its exact localized left symbol h(y,r,η,κ)h(y,r,\eta,\kappa) has the GI3 estimates with orders (a,0)(a,0). Its complete tangential coefficients Hn(r)∈Ψn(FY,EY)H_n(r)\in\Psi^n(F_Y,E_Y), with exact left symbols hnh_n, satisfy, on both real tails |κ|≥CT|\kappa|\geq CT, ∥∂y,rβ∂ηα∂κv(h−∑n=0L−1hnκa−n)∥≤CLαβv|κ|a−L−vTL−|α|.(MH2) \left\|\partial_{y,r}^{\beta}\partial_\eta^{\alpha} \partial_\kappa^v \left(h-\sum_{n=0}^{L-1}h_n\kappa^{a-n}\right)\right\| \leq C_{L\alpha\beta v}|\kappa|^{a-L-v}T^{L-|\alpha|}. \tag{MH2} Its tangentially separated normal amplitudes have the AC2 estimates with the off-diagonal kernels of the same complete HnH_n. Every assertion below is on a compact collar localization, with the exact input density and separate source and target frame factors. A finite chart partition gives the global maps on the unchanged compact boundary.

The first asserted map, for every real tt and s≥0s\geq0, is r+Ae+:H¯(s,t)(Y×ℝ+,FY)→H¯(s−a,t)(Y×ℝ+,EY).(MH3) r^+Ae^+: \overline H_{(s,t)}(Y\times\mathbb R_+,F_Y) \longrightarrow \overline H_{(s-a,t)}(Y\times\mathbb R_+,E_Y). \tag{MH3} The zero extension here is defined as a distribution using the embedding into L2L^2 in the normal variable with tangential Sobolev values proved below. It is not claimed to preserve positive full normal Sobolev order.

The second assertion, for an integer m≥1m\geq1, every real τ\tau, and every real ν\nu, is r+A|{w∈H(−m,τ):supp⁡w⊂Y}:w↦r+Aw∈H¯(ν,τ−m−a−ν).(MH4) \left. r^+A\right|_{\{w\in H_{(-m,\tau)}:\operatorname{supp}w\subset Y\}} : w\longmapsto r^+Aw \in\overline H_{(\nu,\tau-m-a-\nu)}. \tag{MH4} The source in this formula is an actual boundary-supported distribution. This is an all-order special-layer result and does not give ordinary traces of arbitrary volume distributions.

2. An exact upper analytic subtraction with complete tangential coefficients

For an integer L≥1L\geq1, define complete tangential operators successively by U0(r)=H0(r),Un(r)=Hn(r)−∑j=0n−1(a−jn−j)Uj(r)(iΛ)n−j,1≤n<L,Λ=λ(Dy).(MH5) \begin{split} U_0(r)&=H_0(r),\\ U_n(r)&=H_n(r)- \sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\binom{a-j}{n-j} U_j(r)(i\Lambda)^{n-j},\qquad 1\leq n<L, \end{split} \qquad \Lambda=\lambda(D_y). \tag{MH5} All factors in this sum have their displayed order. On a local Euclidean extension, Λ\Lambda is the scalar tangential Fourier multiplier with symbol λ(η)\lambda(\eta). It acts to the right of UjU_j. Thus the exact left symbol of Uj(iΛ)n−jU_j(i\Lambda)^{n-j} is the pointwise expression uj(y,r,η)(iλ(η))n−ju_j(y,r,\eta)(i\lambda(\eta))^{n-j}: the right multiplier has no base-variable dependence, so the exact composition integral, rather than a truncated tangential expansion, gives that equality. In particular Un∈ΨnU_n\in\Psi^n, with every parameter derivative. These are complete operators, including their tangential smoothing terms.

Use the actual finite upper analytic model VL=∑j=0L−1Uj(r)(Dr+iΛ)a−j,vL(y,r,η,κ)=∑j=0L−1uj(y,r,η)(κ+iλ(η))a−j.(MH6) V_L= \sum_{j=0}^{L-1}U_j(r)(D_r+i\Lambda)^{a-j}, \qquad v_L(y,r,\eta,\kappa)= \sum_{j=0}^{L-1}u_j(y,r,\eta)(\kappa+i\lambda(\eta))^{a-j}. \tag{MH6} Every integer power is taken in its literal scalar Fourier multiplier sense. For a nonnegative exponent it is a polynomial; for a negative exponent its only normal pole is −iλ-i\lambda, in the lower half-plane. The model is holomorphic in the upper normal half-plane and uses every coefficient needed for length LL.

The binomial expansion of each summand on |κ|≥C′T|\kappa|\geq C'T, with C′≥2C'\geq2, is (κ+iλ)a−j=∑ℓ=0L−j−1(a−jℓ)(iλ)ℓκa−j−ℓ+rj,L.(MH7) (\kappa+i\lambda)^{a-j} =\sum_{\ell=0}^{L-j-1} \binom{a-j}{\ell}(i\lambda)^\ell\kappa^{a-j-\ell} +r_{j,L}. \tag{MH7} For a negative exponent this is a finite Taylor formula for (1+z)a−j(1+z)^{a-j} on |z|≤1/2|z|\leq1/2, with its integral remainder. For a nonnegative exponent it is the corresponding finite polynomial, retaining any remaining polynomial terms. The differentiated remainder in both cases is bounded by C|κ|a−L−vTL−j−|α|C|\kappa|^{a-L-v}T^{L-j-|\alpha|} before multiplication by uju_j; product differentiation gives the same final bound with TL−|α|T^{L-|\alpha|}. Derivatives of λ\lambda have order 1−|α|1-|\alpha|, obtained by differentiating λ2=1+|η|2\lambda^2=1+|\eta|^2 and induction. Normal derivatives contribute the displayed |κ|−v|\kappa|^{-v}. The finite bounds are uniform for either sign of κ\kappa.

At the coefficient of κa−n\kappa^{a-n}, (MH7) gives un+∑j<n(a−jn−j)uj(iλ)n−j=hnu_n+\sum_{j<n}\binom{a-j}{n-j}u_j(i\lambda)^{n-j}=h_n, exactly (MH5). Therefore the same original coefficients, with every factor, are matched on both tails. Set GL=A−VLG_L=A-V_L. Its full localized symbol satisfies ∥∂y,rβ∂ηα∂κvgL∥≤CLαβvRa−L−vTL−|α|,gL∈Sa−L,L.(MH8) \|\partial_{y,r}^{\beta}\partial_\eta^\alpha \partial_\kappa^v g_L\| \leq C_{L\alpha\beta v} R^{a-L-v}T^{L-|\alpha|}, \qquad g_L\in S^{a-L,L}. \tag{MH8} On the exterior cone this follows from (MH2), (MH7), and R≍|κ|R\asymp|\kappa|. On the remaining region |κ|≤C′T|\kappa|\leq C'T, the exact comparison T≤R≤(1+C′)TT\leq R\leq(1+C')T bounds both the original symbol and each model term by CTa−v−|α|CT^{a-v-|\alpha|}. Since R/TR/T stays between those fixed positive constants, this is precisely the bound on the right of (MH8), for positive or negative exponents. This proves the global estimate and all its derivatives without differentiating RR or TT.

Each model term also lies in Sa,0S^{a,0}. Its direct differentiated bound is CRa−j−vTj−|α|CR^{a-j-v}T^{j-|\alpha|}; the inequality T≤RT\leq R gives the asserted order. The original AA and both parts of its exact decomposition therefore act by the mixed mapping theorem at their stated orders.

Tangential proper support does not remove any coefficient. First localize the original operator as χAψ\chi A\psi, with compact input cutoff ψ\psi. Choose a further compact input cutoff ψ′\psi', equal to one on a neighborhood of its input support. Then (χAψ)ψ′=χAψ(\chi A\psi)\psi'=\chi A\psi exactly, and every complete coefficient obeys Hnψ′=HnH_n\psi'=H_n. Construct the Euclidean model just described for that localized symbol and replace it by VLψ′V_L\psi'. The exact difference is (A−VL)ψ′(A-V_L)\psi'. The mixed composition theorem preserves its order (a−L,L)(a-L,L), while the complete normal coefficient at index nn is Hnψ′=HnH_n\psi'=H_n. Right composition with ψ′\psi' also preserves the normal support relation. This proves compact tangential support and exact coefficient retention together; it does not treat a tangential cutoff error as a smooth full kernel.

To retain proper support, multiply the model kernel by the actual compact normal-difference cutoff, equal to one near zero, and retain the resulting change in GLG_L. This does not change (MH8). Here is the full kernel check. If h≥1h\geq1 and θ=r−s\theta=r-s, inverse Fourier transformation gives ℱκ−1[(κ+iλ)−h](θ)=(−i)h(h−1)!1θ<0(−θ)h−1eλθ.(MH9) {\mathcal F}^{-1}_\kappa [(\kappa+i\lambda)^{-h}](\theta) =\frac{(-i)^h}{(h-1)!} 1_{\theta<0}(-\theta)^{h-1}e^{\lambda\theta}. \tag{MH9} The formula follows from the clockwise lower contour for θ<0\theta<0, including the factor −i-i multiplying the residue and every factor (iθ)h−1(i\theta)^{h-1}; for θ>0\theta>0 the upper contour encloses no pole. It also holds as a tempered distribution by exponential damping, or by applying Dθ+iλD_\theta+i\lambda successively starting with h=1h=1. For a nonnegative integer qq, the exact inverse is ℱκ−1[(κ+iλ)q]=∑v=0q(qv)(iλ)q−vDθvδ0.(MH10) {\mathcal F}^{-1}_\kappa[(\kappa+i\lambda)^q] =\sum_{v=0}^q\binom qv(i\lambda)^{q-v}D_\theta^v\delta_0. \tag{MH10} Thus every model kernel has normal support r−s≤0r-s\leq0. Away from r=sr=s, (MH9) and all its derivatives have arbitrary tangential frequency decay because eλθ≤e−ελe^{\lambda\theta}\leq e^{-\varepsilon\lambda}. Every polynomial tangential factor and every requested derivative is absorbed by this exponential. After the compact localizations, the properness change is a smooth full kernel; it has every mixed order and is retained in GLG_L. The polynomial kernels in (MH10) are supported on the normal diagonal and undergo no change.

For separated tangential chart pieces, use the exact smooth coefficient kernels in AC2. Apply the same triangular recursion with the fixed scalar pole −i-i, and powers (κ+i)a−j(\kappa+i)^{a-j}. All coefficient kernels and all tangential derivatives remain smooth. Matching gives a remainder normal amplitude of order a−La-L; its partial tangential Fourier transform has every negative tangential order by integration by parts in the smooth input variable. In particular it obeys (MH8). Its model still has normal support r−s≤0r-s\leq0. A normal properness change is a smooth full kernel, since the tangential coefficient is already smooth. Finite summation of these exact local and separated constructions gives a global decomposition A=VL+GL,VL∈ℳa,GL∈ℳa−L,L,supp⁡KVL⊂{r≤s}.(MH11) A=V_L+G_L, \qquad V_L\in\mathscr M^a, \qquad G_L\in\mathscr M^{a-L,L}, \qquad \operatorname{supp}K_{V_L}\subset\{r\leq s\}. \tag{MH11} The finite partition and source/target transfers are independent of the normal coordinate and preserve this support relation. No full-kernel or density term is omitted. This is a finite subtraction for each requested estimate, not an infinite patch or a rational replacement for the original operator.

3. The truncated volume map at every original nonnegative normal order

For a full extension uu, its original quadratic norm gives, for s≥0s\geq0, ∥u∥(0,s+t)2=(2π)−(d+1)∫λ2(s+t)|û|2≤(2π)−(d+1)∫Q2sλ2t|û|2=∥u∥(s,t)2.(MH12) \|u\|_{(0,s+t)}^2 =(2\pi)^{-(d+1)}\int \lambda^{2(s+t)}|\widehat u|^2 \leq(2\pi)^{-(d+1)}\int Q^{2s}\lambda^{2t}|\widehat u|^2 =\|u\|_{(s,t)}^2. \tag{MH12} Taking the infimum over full extensions gives the same restriction-space embedding. By normal Plancherel, H(0,s+t)H_{(0,s+t)} is exactly the space with norm (2π)−d∫ℝ∫ℝdλ2(s+t)|ûy(η,r)|2dηdr(2\pi)^{-d}\int_{\mathbb R}\int_{\mathbb R^d}\lambda^{2(s+t)}|\widehat u_y(\eta,r)|^2d\eta\,dr. Zero extension in rr is an isometry from its positive restriction space. Consequently the e+ue^+u in (MH3) belongs to H(0,s+t)H_{(0,s+t)}, with the bound (MH12), even when it fails to belong to H(s,t)H_{(s,t)}.

The normal support relation in (MH11) proves that, at a positive output normal value, VLV_L only uses input normal values at least as large as that output. If two full extensions agree on r>0r>0, their difference has support in r≤0r\leq0; the support of its image under VLV_L is again in r≤0r\leq0. Hence r+VLe+ur^+V_Le^+u is the restriction of VLV_L applied to any full H(s,t)H_{(s,t)} extension. The mixed order (a,0)(a,0) mapping theorem therefore bounds it in H¯(s−a,t)\overline H_{(s-a,t)} by the infimum extension norm of uu.

Choose an integer L≥max⁡(1,s)L\geq\max(1,s). The order (a−L,L)(a-L,L) mapping theorem and (MH12) put GLe+uG_Le^+u in H(L−a,s+t−L)H_{(L-a,s+t-L)}. Its norm controls the desired one, since Qs−aλt≤QL−aλs+t−Lwhen L≥s,QL−aλs+t−LQs−aλt=(Q/λ)L−s≥1.(MH13) Q^{s-a}\lambda^t \leq Q^{L-a}\lambda^{s+t-L} \quad\text{when }L\geq s, \qquad \frac{Q^{L-a}\lambda^{s+t-L}}{Q^{s-a}\lambda^t} =(Q/\lambda)^{L-s}\geq1. \tag{MH13} Restriction and addition in the exact identity (MH11) now prove (MH3). The proof covers the endpoint s=0s=0, any real tangential exponent, negative output normal orders, and all positive ss, without invoking an invalid positive-order zero-extension bound.

4. Boundary-supported distributions and the whole original jet Gram matrix

On a compact tangential localization, a distribution supported at r=0r=0 has a finite normal-jet representation. To prove this, let its distributional order be at most BB on the compact set. A test function whose first B+1B+1 normal jets vanish is O(rB+1)O(r^{B+1}), with the corresponding differentiated estimates. Multiply it by a cutoff χ(r/ε)\chi(r/\varepsilon) equal to one near the support. Every derivative of total order at most BB of that product is O(ε)O(\varepsilon), also after tangential differentiation. The distributional bound makes its pairing tend to zero. The support condition makes the pairing equal to the original one, so it is zero. Subtracting a finite Taylor polynomial times a cutoff therefore expresses the distribution by its first B+1B+1 test jets. Changing from ordinary delta derivatives to Drbδ0=(−i)bδ0(b)D_r^b\delta_0=(-i)^b\delta_0^{(b)} gives unique tangential coefficient distributions.

If w∈H(−m,τ)w\in H_{(-m,\tau)}, its representation has the precise form w=∑b=0m−1fb⊗Drbδ0,fb∈Hτ−m+b+1/2(Y,FY).(MH14) w=\sum_{b=0}^{m-1}f_b\otimes D_r^b\delta_0, \qquad f_b\in H^{\tau-m+b+1/2}(Y,F_Y). \tag{MH14} Here is both the necessity of the range and the exact norm calculation. The Fourier transform is ∑bκbf̂b(η)\sum_b\kappa^b\widehat f_b(\eta). Because the full weighted transform of ww is an actual locally square integrable function, each coefficient is an actual locally square integrable function too: integrate that function against finitely many compactly supported κ\kappa-test functions with an invertible polynomial moment matrix. Such test functions can be chosen using a positive compact cutoff times the monomials; their Gram matrix is positive definite because a nonzero polynomial cannot vanish on an interval. Normal Fubini then identifies the polynomial for almost every η\eta. A nonzero polynomial of degree b≥mb\geq m has infinite squared norm against (λ2+κ2)−mdκ(\lambda^2+\kappa^2)^{-m}d\kappa. Its top coefficient must therefore vanish almost everywhere; descending induction removes all indices at least mm.

For the surviving full polynomial, put Gbc(m)=∫ℝzb+c(1+z2)−mdz,0≤b,c<m,vb(η)=λ(η)bf̂b(η).(MH15) G^{(m)}_{bc}=\int_{\mathbb R}z^{b+c}(1+z^2)^{-m}dz, \quad0\leq b,c<m, \qquad v_b(\eta)=\lambda(\eta)^b\widehat f_b(\eta). \tag{MH15} Every integral is absolutely finite, including b=c=m−1b=c=m-1; its integrand then decays as |z|−2|z|^{-2}. Odd entries vanish by reflection. The whole matrix is Hermitian positive definite, since its quadratic form is the squared integral of the full polynomial. The minimum and maximum on the original finite-coordinate unit sphere are finite positive numbers γ−\gamma_-, γ+\gamma_+, by the proved finite compactness and extrema theorem. No cross term in this matrix is discarded. The exact substitution κ=λz\kappa=\lambda z, keeping all Fourier constants, gives ∥w∥(−m,τ)2=(2π)−(d+1)∫ℝdλ2τ−2m+1v(η)*G(m)v(η)dη,γ−2π∑b=0m−1∥fb∥Hτ−m+b+1/22≤∥w∥(−m,τ)2≤γ+2π∑b=0m−1∥fb∥Hτ−m+b+1/22.(MH16) \begin{split} \|w\|_{(-m,\tau)}^2 &=(2\pi)^{-(d+1)}\int_{\mathbb R^d} \lambda^{2\tau-2m+1}v(\eta)^*G^{(m)}v(\eta)\,d\eta,\\ \frac{\gamma_-}{2\pi}\sum_{b=0}^{m-1} \|f_b\|_{H^{\tau-m+b+1/2}}^2 &\leq\|w\|_{(-m,\tau)}^2 \leq\frac{\gamma_+}{2\pi}\sum_{b=0}^{m-1} \|f_b\|_{H^{\tau-m+b+1/2}}^2. \end{split} \tag{MH16} This proves both directions in (MH14). Compact coordinate changes preserve the norms with their actual finite constants; the normal coordinate and pullback bundle frames are unchanged. If the input density is represented by a nonconstant smooth normal factor, multiplying the supported distribution by that factor uses the full SR5 Leibniz formula, retains every lower delta coefficient, and gives the same finite triangular norm comparison. A finite partition then proves the global representation and its bound.

For one coefficient fbf_b, the operator ADrbA D_r^b has exact left symbol hκbh\kappa^b, belongs to ℒa+b\mathcal L^{a+b}, and retains the same complete tangential coefficient sequence with the shifted normal powers. Apply (MH5)–(MH11) to this actual operator. Its upper model applied to fbδ0f_b\delta_0 has support in r≤0r\leq0, so its positive restriction is zero. Thus its positive layer equals the positive restriction of its remainder of mixed order (a+b−L,L)(a+b-L,L).

Put t*=τ−m−a−νt_* =\tau-m-a-\nu and choose an integer L≥1L\geq1 with ν+a+b−L<−1/2\nu+a+b-L<-1/2.
